title: AKI & ARF: The Renal-Ocular Masterclass
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide to Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and Acute Renal Failure (ARF), bridging systemic emergency management with critical ophthalmic manifestations like TINU, GPA, and medication hazards.

sections.title: Definition & Initial Clinical Triage
content: AKI (formerly Acute Renal Failure/ARF): An abrupt deterioration in renal function occurring over hours or days.
Characterized by: Rising levels of serum creatinine and urea.
Clinical Signs: Often accompanied by oliguria (low urine output) or anuria (absence of urine output).
Initial Approach: Catheterize to assess hourly urine output and establish fluid charts.
Assessment: Check Intravascular Volume (BP, JVP, skin turgor, and weight).
Baseline Labs: U&E, PO₄⁻³, FBC, ESR, CRP, INR, and LFT.
Key Metric: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is more reliable than serum creatinine alone in assessing renal function.

sections.title: The Hyperkalaemia Emergency
content: 1. Identify: Potassium > 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes (Tall, peaked T-waves).
2. Cardioprotection: Calcium Gluconate (10%) 10 mL IV over 2 minutes (Protects heart, does NOT lower K+).
3. Intracellular Shift (Primary): 50 mL of 50% glucose + 10 U fast-acting insulin IV over 30 minutes.
4. Intracellular Shift (Adjunct): Nebulized Salbutamol 2.5 mg.
Critical Pitfall: Calcium gluconate is for stabilization; insulin/glucose is mandatory to actually lower serum potassium.

rows: Bilateral nongranulomatous anterior uveitis; can linger/recur post-nephritis.
Adolescent girls, malaise, proteinuria, elevated β2-microglobulin, abnormal creatinine, WBC casts.
Co-management with nephrologist; High-dose oral corticosteroids.
Chronic rhinitis, focal/segmental glomerulonephritis (80% of cases), renal failure.

sections.title: Shock-Induced AKI (Pre-renal)
content: Diagnosis: Pre-renal ARF due to Hypovolaemic Shock (e.g., Severe upper GI bleeding/haematemesis).
Signs: Cold, clammy skin, thready pulse, BP 90/60.
Action: Secure airway and high-flow O₂.
Access: Insert two wide-bore (14–16G) cannulae.
Resuscitation: Start rapid IV crystalloid (Saline 0.9%).
CRITICAL: If BP remains unrecordable, call the cardiac arrest team.

sections.title: Imaging Hazards & Contrast Safety
content: CT Contrast Pre-check: Must check renal function prior to IV contrast.
Severe Impairment: eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m² carries high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy.
MRI Gadolinium Precaution: In patients >65 with diabetes, check renal function to avoid Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis.
Clinical Pearl: eGFR is the superior marker for deciding on contrast-enhanced imaging.

content.explanation: A: Acidosis (Severe, pH <7.2); E: Electrolytes (Persistent Hyperkalaemia >6 mmol/L); I: Ingestions/Intoxications; O: Overload (Pulmonary edema with no diuresis); U: Uraemia (Uraemic pericarditis or Hypercatabolic renal failure).

rows: Reduced perfusion; often reversible with fluids.
Direct damage to kidney tissue or vasculature.
Blockage of urine outflow; diagnosed by USS.

sections.title: Hypertension, Encephalopathy & SLE
content: Malignant Hypertension: BP 220/120 + Papilloedema. Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles. Requires cautious/gradual BP lowering.
Uraemic Encephalopathy: Confusion, flapping tremor (asterixis), pink palms. Workup: BG, electrolytes, ABG.
Lupus Nephritis (SLE): Malar rash, retinal cotton wool spots, proteinuria. Type 3 hypersensitivity (immune complex) in glomerular basement membrane.
SLE Management: Coordination with rheumatologist; systemic steroids and immunosuppressants (e.g., azathioprine).

sections.title: Glaucoma Meds & Perioperative Hazards
content: Acetazolamide (Diamox): Relatively contraindicated in renal failure. Causes Metabolic Acidosis, Hypokalaemia, and Renal Stones.
Precaution: Check baseline creatinine before starting Acetazolamide in the elderly.
Perioperative (Cataract Surgery): If Creatinine is high (e.g., 180 µmol/L), normal regime continues for LA.
Major Surgery: Monitor electrolytes; AVOID nephrotoxic drugs like NSAIDs and Aminoglycosides.

sections.title: Post-renal, Sepsis & Acidosis
content: Post-renal Obstruction: Sudden anuria + lower abdominal pain. Investigate via USS (look for hydronephrosis). Manage with Catheter or Nephrostomy.
Septic Shock: Bounding pulse, warm skin, low urine output. Rx: Blood cultures -> IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Cefuroxime 1.5g) -> Fluid resuscitation.
Metabolic Acidosis: pH 7.2 + low bicarb. Rx: Ventilation first. Use NaHCO₃ (8.4%) only in severe cases (may worsen intracellular acidosis).

branches: Stabilization: Catheterize (Aim >30 mL/h), Treat Hyperkalaemia (Ca Gluconate/Insulin)
Diagnostic: Urinalysis (Protein, Glucose, RBC/WBC Casts), Imaging (USS/CXR), Blood Profile (U&E, FBC, CRP, ANA, ANCA)

sections.title: Management Pearls & High Yields
content: TINU Pearl: Suspect in any adolescent girl with bilateral anterior uveitis and systemic malaise.
Nephrotoxic Pitfall: Avoid NSAIDs and Aminoglycosides in established renal failure.
GPA High Yield: Renal failure is a major mortality cause (80% 1-year mortality if untreated).
Red Flag: Cushing’s response (low pulse, high BP) with renal signs suggests increased intracranial pressure.
Investigation: c-ANCA is highly sensitive and specific for GPA.
Serum Creatinine Hazard: Contrast media risk is significant in preexisting severe renal impairment.
Investigation: c-ANCA and urinalysis are essential for suspected GPA.

sections.content: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and Acute Renal Failure (ARF): In clinical medicine and emergency settings, Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)—formerly referred to as Acute Renal Failure (ARF)—represents an abrupt deterioration in renal function occurring over hours or days. It is characterized by rising levels of serum creatinine and urea, often accompanied by oliguria (low urine output) or anuria (absence of urine output). Scenario 1: Definition: An acute deterioration in renal function (hours/days) marked by increased serum creatinine/urea and often oliguria or anuria. Initial Approach: Catheterize; Assess Intravascular Volume (BP, JVP, skin turgor, weight); Baseline Labs: U&E, PO4, FBC, ESR, CRP, INR, LFT. eGFR is more reliable than creatinine. Scenario 2: Hyperkalaemia 6.5 mmol/L, peaked T-waves. Rx: Calcium Gluconate (10%) 10 mL IV over 2 min; Insulin 10U + Glucose 50% 50mL over 30 min; Nebulized Salbutamol 2.5mg. Scenario 3: 15yo girl, bilateral nongranulomatous anterior uveitis, malaise, proteinuria, elevated beta2-microglobulin. TINU Syndrome. Rx: Nephrologist, high-dose oral steroids. Scenario 4: GPA/Wegener's: Necrotizing scleritis, chronic rhinitis, renal impairment. Focal/segmental glomerulonephritis (80%). Serum c-ANCA, Urinalysis. Rx: Systemic steroids, cyclophosphamide. Scenario 5: Pre-renal/Hypovolaemic shock. GI bleed, cold clammy skin, thready pulse, BP 90/60. Rx: Airway, O2, 14-16G cannulae, Saline 0.9%. Red Flag: BP unrecordable = cardiac arrest team. Scenario 6: CT Contrast/Gadolinium. eGFR <30 is severe impairment. Gadolinium risk: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in >65 with diabetes. Scenario 7: Urgent Dialysis: K >6, pH <7.2, Pulm edema, Uraemic pericarditis, Hypercatabolic. Scenario 8: Post-renal/Obstruction: Prostate, USS (hydronephrosis), catheter/nephrostomy. Scenario 9: Metabolic Acidosis: pH 7.2, low bicarb. Rx: Ventilation, NaHCO3 8.4% (only in severe cases). Scenario 10: Malignant HTN: 220/120, papilloedema, fibrinoid necrosis. Scenario 11: Acetazolamide: Relatively contraindicated. Causes acidosis, hypokalaemia, stones. Scenario 12: Uraemic Encephalopathy: Confusion, flapping tremor (asterixis), pink palms. Scenario 13: SLE/Lupus Nephritis: Malar rash, CWS, proteinuria, Type 3 hypersensitivity. Scenario 14: Perioperative: Creatinine 180, cataract surgery, avoid NSAIDs/aminoglycosides. Scenario 15: Septic Shock: Bounding pulse, warm skin, low urine. Rx: Antibiotics (Cefuroxime 1.5g), fluids.

data.generationPrompt:
Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and Acute Renal Failure (ARF)
In clinical medicine and emergency settings, Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)—formerly referred to as Acute Renal Failure (ARF)—represents an abrupt deterioration in renal function occurring over hours or days. It is characterized by rising levels of serum creatinine and urea, often accompanied by oliguria (low urine output) or anuria (absence of urine output).
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OSCE & VIVA Clinical Scenarios
Scenario 1: Definition and Initial Triage
Scenario: An examiner asks: "How do you define Acute Renal Failure (ARF) and how do you initiate its management?"
Definition: An acute deterioration in renal function (hours/days) marked by increased serum creatinine/urea and often oliguria or anuria.
Initial Approach:
Catheterize: To assess hourly urine output and establish fluid charts.
Assess Intravascular Volume: Check BP, JVP, skin turgor, and weight.
Baseline Labs: U&E, PO₄⁻³, FBC, ESR, CRP, INR, and LFT.
Key Point: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is more reliable than serum creatinine alone in assessing renal function.
Scenario 2: The Hyperkalaemia Emergency
Scenario: A patient with ARF has a potassium level of 6.5 mmol/L. ECG shows tall, peaked T-waves.
Diagnosis: Life-threatening Hyperkalaemia.
Emergency Management (Drug Doses):
Calcium Gluconate (10%): 10 mL IV over 2 minutes (provides cardioprotection).
Insulin + Glucose: 50 mL of 50% glucose + 10 U fast-acting insulin IV over 30 minutes (shifts K+ into cells).
Nebulized Salbutamol: 2.5 mg to assist K+ shift into cells.
Pitfall: Calcium gluconate protects the heart but does not lower serum potassium levels; insulin/glucose is needed for that.
Scenario 3: Adolescent Uveitis and Renal Signs (TINU)
Scenario: A 15-year-old girl presents with bilateral nongranulomatous anterior uveitis and reported malaise. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and elevated β2-microglobulin.
Diagnosis: Tubulointerstitial Nephritis and Uveitis (TINU) Syndrome.
Key Findings: Abnormal serum creatinine, decreased creatinine clearance, and white cell casts.
Management: Co-management with a nephrologist. Highly responsive to high-dose oral corticosteroids.
Examiner's Pick: Ocular disease can linger or recur long after the resolution of the nephritis.
Scenario 4: GPA and the Kidneys
Scenario: A middle-aged male with necrotizing scleritis and chronic rhinitis is found to have renal impairment.
Diagnosis: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA/Wegener's).
Renal Involvement: Focal and segmental glomerulonephritis, present in 80% of cases, leading to renal failure.
Investigations: Serum c-ANCA (sensitive and specific for GPA) and urinalysis.
Treatment: Systemic steroids and immunosuppressants (typically cyclophosphamide).
Scenario 5: Pre-renal AKI (Hypovolaemic Shock)
Scenario: A patient with severe upper GI bleeding (haematemesis) presents with cold, clammy skin, thready pulse, and a BP of 90/60.
Diagnosis: Pre-renal ARF due to Hypovolaemic Shock.
Management: Secure airway and high-flow O₂. Insert two wide-bore (14–16G) cannulae and start rapid IV crystalloid (Saline 0.9%).
Red Flag: If BP remains unrecordable, call the cardiac arrest team.
Scenario 6: Interpretations - Creatinine vs. eGFR
Scenario: A 76-year-old patient is scheduled for CT with IV contrast.
Critical Action: Check renal function prior to contrast. eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m² indicates severe renal impairment.
Hazard: IV contrast media carries a risk in patients with preexisting severe renal impairment.
Precaution: In patients >65 with diabetes, renal function must be checked before Gadolinium-enhanced MRI to avoid nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
Scenario 7: Indications for Urgent Dialysis
Scenario: You are managing a patient with ARF. The examiner asks: "When is dialysis mandatory?"
Criteria for Urgent Dialysis:
Persistent hyperkalaemia (>6 mmol/L).
Severe acidosis (pH <7.2).
Pulmonary edema with no diuresis.
Uraemic pericarditis.
Hypercatabolic renal failure.
Scenario 8: Post-renal AKI (Obstruction)
Scenario: An elderly male with a history of prostate issues presents with sudden cessation of urine and lower abdominal pain.
Diagnosis: Post-renal ARF due to Obstruction.
Investigation: Ultrasound scan (USS) of the renal tract to identify obstruction (e.g., hydronephrosis).
Management: Immediate catheterization or nephrostomy.
Scenario 9: Metabolic Acidosis in ARF
Scenario: A patient in a coma has an ABG showing a pH of 7.2 and low bicarbonate.
Diagnosis: Metabolic Acidosis secondary to Renal Failure.
Management: Good ventilation to treat acidosis; use sodium bicarbonate (8.4%) only in severe cases after prolonged resuscitation as it can worsen intracellular acidosis.
Scenario 10: Hypertensive Urgency and the Kidneys
Scenario: A patient presents with a BP of 220/120 and papilloedema.
Diagnosis: Malignant/Accelerated Hypertension.
Renal Complication: End-organ damage due to fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles.
Management: Immediate medical referral for cautious and gradual BP lowering to avoid precipitating renal or cerebral ischaemia.
Scenario 11: Side Effects of Glaucoma Meds (Acetazolamide)
Scenario: An elderly patient with moderate renal impairment is given oral Acetazolamide for high IOP.
Hazard: Acetazolamide is relatively contraindicated in renal failure.
Side Effects: Metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, and renal stones.
Precaution: Check baseline creatinine before initiation.
Scenario 12: Uraemic Encephalopathy
Scenario: A patient with known renal failure presents with confusion, flapping tremor (asterixis), and pink palms.
Diagnosis: Uraemic encephalopathy leading to coma.
Workup: Blood glucose (rule out hypoglycemia), electrolytes, and ABG.
Scenario 13: AKI in SLE (Lupus Nephritis)
Scenario: A young woman with a malar rash and retinal cotton wool spots has proteinuria.
Diagnosis: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) with renal involvement.
Key Points: Type 3 hypersensitivity (immune complex deposition) in the glomerular basement membrane.
Management: Requires coordination with a rheumatologist for systemic steroids and immunosuppressants (e.g., azathioprine).
Scenario 14: Perioperative Care for the Renal Patient
Scenario: A patient with a creatinine of 180 µmol/L is scheduled for cataract surgery.
Perioperative Management: Normal or near-normal regime can continue for local anesthesia. For major surgery, monitor electrolytes closely and avoid nephrotoxic drugs like NSAIDs and aminoglycosides.
Scenario 15: Septic Shock and AKI
Scenario: A patient presents with a bounding pulse, warm skin, and low urine output.
Diagnosis: Septic Shock causing AKI.
Management: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., Cefuroxime 1.5g) after blood cultures. Fluid resuscitation with colloids or crystalloids.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Classifications of Acute Renal Failure
Category
Causes
Key Features
Pre-renal
Hypovolaemia (bleeding, burns), Low COP (heart failure)
Reduced perfusion to kidneys; often reversible with fluids.
Renal (Intrinsic)
Glomerulonephritis, drugs, vasculitis (GPA, SLE), sepsis
Direct damage to kidney tissue or vasculature.
Post-renal
Obstruction (calculi, tumors, prostate)
Blockage of urine outflow; diagnosed by USS.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Workup & Approach Mind Map: The ARF Algorithm
Immediate Assessment (ABC & Safety):
Assess consciousness (AVPU/GCS).
Check Vital Signs (Tachycardia/Hypotension).
Stabilization Phase:
Catheterize: Monitor hourly urine (Aim >30 mL/h).
Treat Hyperkalaemia: Calcium gluconate → Insulin/Glucose.
Diagnostic Phase:
Urinalysis: Check for protein (nephritis), glucose (DM), or WBC/RBC casts.
Imaging: USS for obstruction; CXR for lung-renal syndromes (GPA/Sarcoid).
Blood Profile: U&E, FBC, ESR/CRP, Autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA).
Specialist Referral:
Refer to Nephrology/Neurosurgery if obstruction or biopsy needed.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Management Pearls, Pitfalls & High Yields
Pearl: TINU should be considered in any adolescent girl with bilateral anterior uveitis and systemic malaise.
Pitfall: Avoid NSAIDs and Aminoglycosides in patients with established renal failure as they are nephrotoxic.
Examiner's Pick: eGFR is a superior marker for renal function over creatinine, especially when deciding on contrast-enhanced imaging.
High Yield: In GPA, renal failure is a major cause of mortality if untreated (80% 1-year mortality).
Red Flag: Cushing’s response (low pulse, high BP) in a patient with renal signs suggests increased intracranial pressure.
Precaution: Acetazolamide should be used with extreme caution in patients with renal insufficiency due to the high risk of metabolic acidosis.
